t: The Natufians lived by hunting and gathering, yet their settlements were larger and more permanent than any before them, some with round stone houses and the first known food stores.
They cut wild cereals with stone sickles and made a bread-like food thousands of years before farming, and they may be the ancestors of the builders of the Levant’s first Neolithic settlements.
Dorothy Garrod named the culture in 1929 after the Wadi Natuf; ancient DNA shows that later Levantines descend mainly from the Natufians.
dyk: At ʿAin Mallaha in Israel, about 12,000 BCE, an elderly person was buried together with a puppy four to five months old.
ev: A pita-like bread of wild cereal seeds and tubers is made, among the oldest known bread-like foods
A woman of apparent importance is buried in a ceremonial pit in Hilazon Tachtit cave
At ʿAin Mallaha an elderly person is buried with a puppy
The Late Natufian begins, in step with the cold, dry Younger Dryas
The Natufian period ends at the very beginning of the Holocene
Dorothy Garrod excavates Shuqba Cave and finds a layer of microliths between Upper Palaeolithic and Bronze Age deposits
After finding similar material at el-Wad, Garrod names the Natufian culture after the Wadi Natuf
Residues of 13,000-year-old beer are reported from a cave near Haifa

f.homeland: The Levant: mostly Israel and the Palestinian territories, also Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, the Sinai Peninsula and the Negev; key sites Shuqba Cave, el-Wad, Ain Mallaha, Hayonim Cave, Hilazon Tachtit, Raqefet Cave, Nahal Ein Gev II, Tell Abu Hureyra, Shubayqa 1
f.period: c. 15,000–11,500 years before present; radiocarbon dates of c. 12,500–9,500 BCE; Early Natufian c. 12,000–10,800 BCE, Late Natufian c. 10,800–9,500 BCE (in step with the Younger Dryas)
f.known: settled or semi-settled villages before agriculture; the earliest known food storage; the first sickle blades; the oldest known bread-like food; possible early beer-brewing; burials with dogs; the Hilazon Tachtit grave; the Ain Sakhri lovers
f.sources: Excavated cave and open-air sites (around 90 excavated), stone and bone tools, plant and animal remains, burials and grave goods, radiocarbon dating and ancient DNA studies
